entry.title: Did Jimi Hendrix Change Music Forever?
entry.summary:
Jimi Hendrix was a true musical innovator who revolutionised the world of music with his groundbreaking guitar techniques, genre-bending compositions, and socially conscious lyrics. His impact on music cannot be overstated and his legacy continues to inspire and captivate audiences around the world. Whether you're a die-hard fan or simply appreciate great music, there's no denying the enduring power and influence of this legendary artist.

More
entry.content:
Jimi Hendrix is widely regarded as one of the most influential and innovative guitarists of all time. His music continues to inspire new generations of musicians and fans alike, and his impact on the world of music cannot be overstated. In this post, we'll take a closer look at some of the reasons why Hendrix was such a groundbreaking and important figure in music history.

  1. Innovative Guitar Techniques

One of the most significant ways in which Jimi Hendrix revolutionized music was through his innovative guitar techniques. He was known for his use of feedback, distortion, and other effects, which helped to create a completely new sound. Hendrix's playing style was characterised by his incredible technical proficiency, as well as his ability to coax new sounds out of his guitar that had never been heard before.

  1. Blending Genres

Another way in which Hendrix was an innovator was through his ability to blend different genres of music together. He was not content to simply play the blues or rock and roll; instead, he drew from a wide range of influences, including funk, soul, R&B, and jazz. By combining these genres, Hendrix was able to create a sound that was entirely his own, and that would go on to influence countless other musicians.

  1. Experimental Songwriting

Hendrix was also a true innovator when it came to songwriting. He was not content to simply follow the standard verse-chorus-verse structure that was prevalent in popular music at the time. Instead, he experimented with different song structures, incorporating elements of improvisation and experimentation into his compositions. This approach helped to create a sense of spontaneity and energy in his music that was truly unique.

  1. Social and Political Consciousness

Finally, Hendrix was an innovator in terms of his social and political consciousness. He was not content to simply make music for the sake of entertainment; instead, he used his platform to speak out about issues that were important to him, such as the civil rights movement and the Vietnam War. This made him a powerful voice for change, and helped to inspire a generation of musicians and fans to think critically about the world around them.

In conclusion, Jimi Hendrix was one of the biggest musical innovators ever for a multitude of reasons. He pushed the boundaries of what was possible on the guitar, blending different genres of music together, experimenting with song structures, and using his platform to speak out about important social and political issues. His impact on the world of music cannot be overstated, and his legacy continues to inspire new generations of musicians and fans alike.

entry.title: Stevie Ray Vaughan: The Legend Who Lives On
entry.summary:
Stevie Ray Vaughan's guitar skills were truly legendary, and his passion for the blues was contagious. His life may have been cut short, but his music continues to live on, inspiring new generations of guitarists around the world.

More
entry.content:
Stevie Ray Vaughan is undoubtedly one of the greatest guitarists to ever grace the world of music. His influence can still be felt today, long after his untimely death in 1990. Vaughan's virtuosic playing, soulful vocals, and passion for the blues have earned him a place in the pantheon of guitar legends. In this blog post, we will take a look at why Stevie Ray Vaughan is so legendary, and what makes him an icon. 

Stevie Ray Vaughan was born in Dallas, Texas, in 1954. He began playing the guitar at the age of 7, and quickly developed a love for the blues. As a teenager, he played in local bands, and in the early 1970s, he formed his own band, Triple Threat Revue. Vaughan's talent soon caught the attention of other musicians, and he was invited to join several bands, including Marc Benno and the Nightcrawlers and Paul Ray and the Cobras.

It was in 1982 that Vaughan's career really took off. He formed the band Double Trouble, and released their debut album, "Texas Flood." The album was a huge success, and Vaughan's incredible guitar playing earned him critical acclaim and a devoted fanbase. Over the next several years, Vaughan continued to release hit albums, including "Couldn't Stand the Weather" and "Soul to Soul." He also collaborated with other musicians, including his brother Jimmie Vaughan, and Eric Clapton.

Vaughan's guitar playing was truly legendary. He was a master of the blues, and his solos were filled with emotion and technical skill. His style was influenced by the great blues guitarists of the past, including Albert King, B.B. King, and Jimi Hendrix, but he also had his own unique sound. Vaughan played with incredible speed and precision, and he could make his guitar sing like no one else.

Vaughan's passion for the blues was also a big part of his legend. He was a true student of the genre, and he studied the great blues musicians of the past. He was also a great champion of the blues, and he helped to bring the genre to a wider audience. Vaughan's love of the blues was evident in every note he played, and his performances were always filled with soul and emotion.

In addition to his incredible guitar playing and love of the blues, Vaughan was also an incredibly charismatic performer. He had a natural charm and charisma that made him a favourite of fans around the world. He was a dynamic and engaging performer, and his concerts were always electrifying.

Sadly, Stevie Ray Vaughan's life was cut short when he died in a helicopter crash in 1990, at the age of 35. However, his legacy lives on, and his influence can still be heard in the playing of countless guitarists around the world. His music continues to inspire new generations of musicians, and his place in the pantheon of guitar legends is secure.

In conclusion, Stevie Ray Vaughan is a true guitar legend. His incredible playing, his love of the blues, and his charismatic personality all helped to make him a true icon of the music world. He deserves to be celebrated for his incredible talent, and for the enormous influence he had on the world of music.

With their swirling, pulsing tones, these pedals have carved out their place in the pantheon of effects, inspiring generations of guitarists and making us wonder: what would our favourite songs sound like without them?

More
entry.content:
The Univibe guitar pedal is one of the most iconic effects of the 1960s. It was originally developed in the late 1960s by the Japanese company Shin-ei as a rotating speaker simulator. However, it quickly found its way into the hands of guitarists who were looking for something different than the standard fuzz and wah sounds that dominated the era.

The Univibe was famously used by Jimi Hendrix on tracks like "Machine Gun" and "Star Spangled Banner," as well as by David Gilmour on Pink Floyd's "Breathe" and "Echoes." Its unique sound has been emulated by countless pedals and plugins over the years, but there's nothing quite like the original.

The Univibe uses a combination of phasing and vibrato to create its distinctive sound. The effect is warm, smooth, and almost hypnotic, with a pulsating quality that's hard to describe. It's perfect for creating spacey, psychedelic textures, but it can also be used to add a subtle, watery vibe to clean or overdriven tones.

It can be used as a clean boost, an overdrive, or a distortion pedal, depending on how you set the controls. It can be used to push your amp into overdrive, to add sustain to your solos, or to give your clean sound a little bit of grit.

Its influence can be heard in countless recordings and live performances, and it has inspired a whole generation of guitarists to experiment with overdrive and distortion. The Roger Mayer Octavia is an iconic guitar effects pedal that has left an indelible mark on the sound of rock and roll.   1. It was used by Jimi Hendrix.

One of the main reasons why the Octavia is so iconic is its association with Jimi Hendrix. Hendrix used the pedal on many of his most famous recordings, including "Purple Haze" and "Fire." The pedal was created by Roger Mayer specifically for Hendrix, and its unique sound helped define the sound of psychedelic rock in the late 1960s. Hendrix's use of the Octavia helped establish it as an essential component of the electric guitar's sonic vocabulary and contributed to its legendary status.

  1. It produces a unique sound.

The Octavia produces an octave-up effect that creates a higher-pitched sound that is one octave above the original note. This effect is not found in nature, and it gives the pedal a unique and distinctive sound that has made it a favourite among guitarists. The Octavia also adds distortion and sustain to the guitar's sound, creating a powerful and dynamic tone that can be used in many different musical contexts. The pedal's versatility and unique sound have helped make it an iconic component of the guitar player's toolkit.

  1. It has been used by countless guitar legends.

The Octavia has been used by many of the greatest guitarists in history, including Jeff Beck, Eric Johnson, and Stevie Ray Vaughan. Its association with these guitar legends has helped establish it as an iconic pedal that is essential to the sound of rock and roll. The pedal's ability to produce a wide range of sounds and its unique tonal characteristics have made it a favourite among guitarists in many different genres, from rock and blues to funk and beyond.

  1. It has stood the test of time.

The Octavia was originally created in the late 1960s, but it continues to be a popular pedal today. Its timeless sound and versatility have helped it stand the test of time and remain an essential component of the modern guitar sound. Roger Mayer has continued to update the pedal over the years, ensuring that it remains relevant and accessible to new generations of guitarists. The Klon Centaur is a highly sought-after guitar overdrive pedal that was designed and built by Bill Finnegan in the mid-1990s. Its reputation has only grown over the years, with a devoted following of guitarists who swear by its sound and its unique ability to enhance the natural sound of a guitar.

One of the reasons for the Klon Centaur's popularity is its versatility. The pedal is designed to provide a transparent overdrive tone that can be used for a wide range of musical styles and genres. From clean boosts and light overdrive to heavy distortion and everything in between, the Klon Centaur can do it all.

Famous guitarists have helped to cement the Klon Centaur's reputation as a must-have pedal. John Mayer is one such musician who is known for using the Klon Centaur. As one of the most accomplished and celebrated guitarists of his generation, Mayer's endorsement of the pedal has added to its allure and helped to keep it in the conversation as one of the greatest overdrive pedals of all time. Mayer has spoken about the pedal in interviews, highlighting its ability to add warmth and depth to his already impressive tone.

Another reason for the Klon Centaur's popularity is its build quality. The pedal was handmade by Bill Finnegan himself, using high-quality components and a meticulous attention to detail. This gave the Klon Centaur a reputation for being an incredibly well-made and reliable pedal, which is highly valued by guitarists who rely on their equipment for live performances and recording sessions.

The rarity of the Klon Centaur is also a factor in its popularity. The pedal was only produced in limited numbers during its initial run, and Bill Finnegan stopped making them in the early 2000s. This has led to a situation where demand for the pedal far outstrips supply, and it is now highly sought-after on the vintage market, with prices reaching into the thousands of dollars.

Despite the high price tag and rarity of the Klon Centaur, many guitarists continue to use it as their go-to overdrive pedal, citing its unique sound and build quality as reasons for their loyalty. If you're looking for a versatile overdrive pedal that can be used in a variety of musical styles and genres, the Klon Centaur is well worth seeking out. entry.title: Why is John Mayer so HATED?!
entry.content:
Hey guys, in this blog post, we're going to be discussing one of the most polarizing characters in music history - John Mayer.

John Mayer's notoriety is perhaps due to his upbringing as a child prodigy guitarist with unparalleled talent. He was often compared to idols like Steve Ray Vaughan and Jimi Hendrix, which made some fans feel like he was almost betraying their legacy. In addition to this, some fans faulted him for using new cutting-edge technology such as digital modeling as opposed to tried and true analogue guitar pedals and amps. It's almost like everything John Mayer touches turns into a polarizing ideology because even the PRS silver sky, which is designed by John Mayer, has recently been one of the most controversial guitars in recent history. People either simply love it or hate it.

Mayer would also incorporate musical genres such as hip-hop, rap, and blues all together in a way that felt strange and unfamiliar to a lot of fans. There also seems to be this underlying notion that John Mayer is too big for his boots. If you ever watch any interviews with John Mayer, he's certainly not shy, and he has incredible comedic timing, rubbing people up the wrong way left, right, and center. You can't go to any comment section about John Mayer without there being two camps - ones that absolutely love him and ones that just despise him.

From music festivals and arena tours to collaborating with huge names like Alicia Keys and just everyone you can think of, John has undoubtedly scored huge successes throughout his career. This could certainly have caused huge resentment, especially among aspiring guitarists trying to make it and not getting anywhere. I feel like this has led to a lot of guitarists feeling almost overshadowed by his successes.

Another detail that has caused some resentment towards John Mayer is the fact that he seems to be living a life of pure luxury and privilege. From Dumble amps to watches worth hundreds of thousands of pounds to private jets to then dating absolute beautiful supermodels and actresses, it's no wonder why a lot of guitarists are salty about John Mayer. But that can also lead to the perception that he's now been granted everything that he ever wanted, therefore he's lost his true artistry.

Finally, there are those who claim that Mayer's interpretations of classics like Voodoo Child and Little Wing do not live up to the originals. Although a lot of critics have actually praised these covers, many feel that these original versions are in fact untouchable.

Overall, I think it's pretty safe to say that John Mayer will never win over everyone with his style and his music. He will remain a highly polarizing figure within the music scene with both passionate admirers and fierce opponents. This doesn't stop with John Mayer - every musician, brand, or whoever it might be online or anywhere in the world will have their admirers and their detractors. This is just part of someone trying to build something for themselves.

entry.title: Uncovering the Marshall Reissues - Guv'nor, Shred Master, Drive Master & Blues Breaker
entry.summary:
The discovery of four unreleased Marshall Vintage reissue pedals, including the Blues Breaker, Guv'nor, Shred Master, and Drive Master. These pedals were obtained through a leaked pre-order link...

More
entry.content:
The bizarre Marshall story continues... as we recently got our hands on something very exciting - four unreleased Marshall Vintage Reissue pedals that have not even been confirmed by Marshall yet! You might have seen a video we did recently of the brand new unreleased Marshall Bluesbreaker Vintage Reissue, which has been picked up by guitar articles such as Music Radar. But the story doesn't end there - we were then contacted by a mysterious figure claiming to have gotten their hands on the much-speculated reissues of not only the Bluesbreaker, but also the Drive Master, Shred Master, and the Marshall Guv'nor, which would complete the Marshall Black Box series of reissues.

At first, we were skeptical about these three other reissues, as we hadn't heard anything online about them, and there was no confirmation from Marshall, and no pictures of them on Instagram. However, it turned out that the mysterious figure was telling the truth, and had bought them in the exact same way we bought the Marshall Bluesbreaker last year - through the accidental pre-order link leaked by Thomann.

We were excited to hear what these pedals sounded like for the very first time, and decided to unbox them for you here:

The product boxes are beautiful and look identical to the original Marshall boxes. I actually prefer them to the originals! We started with the Marshall Guv'nor, and the pedal is housed in a casing that is accurately modeled on the design of the original, from the unique shape right down to the individually colored control knobs. The reissue manual tells us that the original Guv'nor pedal was released in 1988 and set the bar for generations of distortion pedals that have followed since. This 60th anniversary reissue (from the original formation date of Marshall) faithfully recreates the classic sound of the Guv'nor, providing a smooth overdrive sound with a touch of compression.

Next, we unboxed the Marshall Shred Master, which is also housed in a beautiful box. The Shred Master was originally released in 1992, & the reissue manual tells us that the Shred Master reissue features the original tone that helped shaped many bands over the last 3 decades!

The third pedal we unboxed was the Marshall Drive Master, which again was originally released in 1992. The Drive Master is essentially an aesthetically updated Guv'nor! Same great sound, though visually in keeping with the other 90's bad boys!

Last but not least, we unboxed the Marshall Bluesbreaker Vintage Reissue, which we have already covered in a previous video here:

In conclusion, it was an absolute pleasure to unbox these four amazing pedals, and we can't wait to demo them in even more depth soon. It's still a mystery as to when these pedals will be officially released by Marshall, but we will keep you updated on any news we hear.

entry.title: Gibson VS Fender (DEBATE SETTLED)

More
entry.content:
For many guitar enthusiasts, the Gibson versus Fender debate is a never-ending discussion. These two brands have produced some of the most legendary guitars in history, each with a unique sound and style. While it's true that both companies have created some exceptional instruments, they differ significantly in terms of design, tone, and style. Let's dive into the details and explore what each brand has to offer.

Gibson Guitars:

Gibson is known for producing some of the most iconic electric guitars in history, such as the Les Paul, SG, and Explorer. These guitars are made from high-quality woods, have thicker necks, and tend to be heavier than Fenders. Gibson's guitars deliver a rich, warm tone that is perfect for blues, rock, and heavy metal music. The Les Paul, in particular, is famous for its thick, creamy sound, which is achieved through its solid mahogany body and set-in neck design. Gibson guitars are also known for their impeccable craftsmanship, with their attention to detail being unmatched. Their use of premium materials and construction techniques makes Gibson guitars a must-have for anyone looking for a quality instrument.

Fender Guitars:

Fender, on the other hand, is known for producing guitars that have a brighter, more twangy sound. The Stratocaster, Telecaster, and Jazzmaster are some of Fender's most iconic models, and they are often associated with genres like country, blues, and rock. Fender's guitars feature bolt-on necks and single-coil pickups, which give them a more trebly sound that cuts through the mix. Fender also offers a wider variety of body shapes and colors to choose from, which can be a big selling point for some players. Their guitars are also known for their comfortable playability, with thinner necks and lighter bodies making them ideal for players who prefer a sleeker design.

Check out this A/B test we did with both brands most iconic models, the Les Paul & Stratocaster!

Which One Is Better?

When it comes to deciding which brand is better, it ultimately comes down to personal preference and the style of music you play. If you're into heavy, distorted tones, you might prefer a Gibson. If you're more of a clean player who likes to pick out every note, you might prefer a Fender. However, both brands have a loyal following and have contributed to some of the most iconic music in history. It's all about finding the guitar that fits your playing style and musical taste.

Conclusion:

In conclusion, Gibson and Fender are both exceptional guitar brands that have stood the test of time. Each has a distinct style and tone that has made them favorites among musicians for generations. Choosing between the two ultimately comes down to your personal preference, but rest assured that whichever one you choose, you'll be getting a high-quality instrument that will serve you well for years to come.

entry.title: Guitar Pedal Signal Chain Order (The Definitive Guide)
entry.summary:
Transform your guitar sound with the right pedal order. Unlock new levels of creativity and achieve your desired tone by following our guidelines...

More
entry.content:
As a guitarist, you know that the order of effects pedals in your signal chain can have a big impact on the overall sound of your guitar. While there's no one-size-fits-all approach to ordering your pedals, there are some general guidelines that can help you achieve the tone you're looking for. In this post, we'll discuss the best way to order your guitar pedal signal chain, including where to place fuzz and treble boosters.

Understanding Pedal Roles

First, it's important to understand the basic types of pedals and their functions. The most common types of pedals are:

  1. Dynamics pedals: These include compressors, limiters, and volume pedals, and they help to control the dynamics of your guitar's signal.

  2. Filter pedals: These include wah-wah pedals and envelope filters, and they can shape the frequency content of your guitar's signal.

  3. Fuzz and distortion pedals: These include overdrive, distortion, and fuzz pedals, and they can add grit and distortion to your guitar's signal.

  4. Treble boosters: These boost the treble frequencies of your guitar's signal, adding clarity and cutting through the mix.

  5. Modulation pedals: These include chorus, flanger, and phaser pedals, and they can create movement and depth in your guitar's signal.

  6. Time-based effects: These include delay and reverb pedals, and they can add depth and ambience to your guitar's signal.

With that in mind, here's a recommended order for your guitar pedal signal chain:

  1. Fuzz and treble boosters: If you're using a fuzz or treble booster pedal, you'll want to place it first in your signal chain. These pedals interact with your guitar's pickups and can help shape your tone before it even hits your other pedals.

  2. Dynamics pedals: These should come next. Compressors and limiters help to even out your guitar's volume, while volume pedals can be used to control your overall volume level.

  3. Filter pedals: These should come next. Wah-wah pedals and envelope filters can shape your guitar's frequency content and create interesting tonal variations.

  4. Distortion pedals: These should come after your dynamics and filter pedals. Overdrive pedals produce a smooth, bluesy distortion, while distortion pedals produce a harder-edged sound.

  5. Modulation pedals: These should come next. Chorus, flanger, and phaser pedals create movement and depth in your guitar's signal. They work best after overdrive and distortion pedals, as they can be affected by the gain in those pedals.

  6. Time-based effects: These should be last in your signal chain. Delay and reverb pedals add depth and ambience to your guitar's signal, and they work best when placed after all other effects.

Uni-Vibe Style Pedals:

Now, let's talk about Uni-Vibe pedals. These produce a unique swirling, vibrato-like effect that can add depth and texture to your guitar's signal. There are a couple of ways to incorporate them into your signal chain:

  1. Before fuzz/overdrive: If you want that big, fat, watery sound that's reminiscent of Robin Trower, you can place your vibe pedal before your fuzz or overdrive pedal. This will create a thick, saturated sound that's perfect for solos and leads.

  2. After fuzz/overdrive: If you want a more classic rock sound that's reminiscent of Jimi Hendrix at Woodstock, you can place your vibe pedal after your fuzz or overdrive pedal. This will create a more swooshing, swirling effect that adds depth and texture to your distorted sound.

Overview

Of course, this is just a starting point, and there are no hard and fast rules when it comes to pedal order. Experimentation is key, and you may find that certain combinations of pedals sound better in a different order. As a general rule, however, following the signal chain outlined above will help you achieve a clear, balanced, and well-defined tone that allows each effect to work to its fullest potential.

entry.title: Silicon vs Germanium Transistors (FUZZ Pedals Explained)
entry.summary:
It's time to dive into the world of Fuzz pedals and discover the differences between Silicon and Germanium Transistors!

More
entry.content:
Fuzz pedals are a popular type of guitar effects pedal that use transistor technology to produce a distorted, fuzzy sound. Silicon and germanium transistors are two common types of transistors used in fuzz pedals, and they have distinct differences that affect the tone and performance of the pedal. In this blog post, we will explore these differences in more detail.

What is a Transistor?

Transistors are electronic devices that can amplify and switch electronic signals. In a fuzz pedal, they are used to amplify the guitar's signal and then clip the waveform, creating a distorted and fuzzy sound. Silicon and germanium are two materials commonly used to make transistors, and they have different properties that affect their performance.

Silicon

Silicon transistors are more commonly used in modern fuzz pedals, and they have a high gain and a tighter, more controlled distortion. Silicon transistors can handle high levels of current and voltage, making them suitable for high-gain and high-output applications. They also have a wider frequency response, which means they can produce a more extended range of tones.

Here's a sound example with our Pedal Pawn Fuzz (SILICON)

Germanium

On the other hand, germanium transistors are an older technology and are known for producing a warmer, smoother, and more organic distortion. Germanium transistors have a lower gain and are more sensitive to temperature and voltage changes. This can make them unpredictable, but it also gives them a more dynamic and expressive character. Germanium transistors also have a more limited frequency response, which can result in a more vintage or retro sound.

 Here's a sound example with our Pedal Pawn Fuzz (GERMANIUM)

Clean-Up

In addition to the differences in their distortion characteristics, silicon and germanium transistors also interact differently with a guitar's volume knob when it comes to clean up. As a general rule, silicon transistors have a more glassy clean up, while germanium transistors are a bit more woody. This means that when you roll off your guitar's volume knob with a fuzz pedal that uses silicon transistors, the distortion will clean up in a more transparent and clear way, whereas with a fuzz pedal that uses germanium transistors, the clean up will have a warmer, more organic character. This can be a significant factor to consider when choosing between silicon and germanium transistors for a fuzz pedal, depending on the type of tone and playing style you prefer.

Power Supply

One important consideration when choosing between silicon and germanium transistors for a fuzz pedal is the power supply. Germanium transistors are more sensitive to voltage changes, and this is one of the reasons that batteries are often recommended for pedals of this nature.

Summary

In summary, silicon and germanium transistors have distinct differences that affect their performance in fuzz pedals. Silicon transistors are more commonly used in modern pedals and offer a tighter, more controlled distortion with a wider frequency response. Germanium transistors, on the other hand, are known for producing a warmer, more organic distortion with a more limited frequency response. When choosing between silicon and germanium transistors for a fuzz pedal, it is important to consider the desired tone and performance characteristics you're trying to achieve.

entry.title: Marshall BluesBreaker Pedal Reissue (FIRST LOOK)
entry.summary:
We are the first company to demo the elusive BluesBreaker REISSUE, read on to hear about this bizarre story...

More
entry.content:
We are the first company to demo the elusive BluesBreaker REISSUE, read on to hear about this bizarre story...

For a bit of context, at the time of writing this blog, the reissue is STILL not technically released to the public. 

The Marshall BluesBreaker guitar pedal is well-known for its use by the renowned guitarist John Mayer. I talk in the video below about a reissue of the pedal that was accidentally made available for pre-order by Thomann, a European retailer, around a year ago. Despite Marshall denying the existence of a reissue, we decided to purchase it anyway. We were confused about whether it was a scam or not, but later received an update from Thomann that the product was on back order and would ship once they were in stock.

The original pedals were initially inexpensive and could be bought for around £50 or £60. However, when pictures of John Mayer's pedalboard featuring the pedal started circulating, the price skyrocketed to an all-time high of around £600 on the resale market.

I wonder whether the reissue's launch will affect the price of the original. Overall, I am very impressed with the reissue and suggest that guitar enthusiasts might want to get their hands on it once released, especially given its presumed lower price compared to the original.

Check out the tones here:

Shootout!

In the following video, we do the ultimate shootout between the original MK1 Bluesbreaker from the 90s, and the brand new, still technically unreleased Marshall Bluesbreaker reissue. I use the exact same settings and go back and forth to do the truest A/B test possible.

The original Bluesbreaker had two different types of circuits over a period of time, the MK1 1.1 and the MK1 1.2 circuit, and the reissue circuit is a part-for-part reissue of the 1.1 circuit.

I start off the shootout with the settings at noon just to get used to the feel of the pedal and see how it operates. As expected, there's not much output or juice going on with these settings (as per the original). But as the volume gets cranked up, the pedal starts to get more into that Blues Breaker territory that everyone knows and loves the sound of.

In my opinion, the reissue delivers pretty much identically to the old one. I can't hear a difference in this demo. 

I am blown away by these reissues, and for the 130 pounds we paid for it, it's an incredible score, especially for the construction of a pedal that is as well-made as the original. The only difference between these two pedals is the boxes, which are aesthetically completely different. 

What do you think to the sound here? Can you hear a difference?

entry.title: Rosewood VS Maple Neck (SOLVED!)
entry.summary:
Looking for the perfect electric guitar neck? The choice of wood can make all the difference. Discover the differences between maple and rosewood necks, and find the perfect fit for your playing style and sound preferences.

More
entry.content:
When it comes to electric guitars, there are a lot of factors that go into their tone, playability, and aesthetics. One of the key elements of a guitar's construction is the neck, and specifically, the choice of wood for the neck can have a significant impact on the instrument's overall sound and feel. Two of the most popular choices for guitar necks are maple and rosewood, each with its own distinct properties and benefits. In this blog post, we'll explore the differences between maple and rosewood guitar necks, and help you determine which one might be the best fit for you.

Maple Neck

Maple is a dense, hard, and stiff wood that is often used for guitar necks due to its strength and stability. Maple necks are typically lighter in color than rosewood necks, with a smooth, clear finish that shows off the wood's natural grain patterns. Maple necks are also known for their bright, snappy tone, which is characterized by strong upper-midrange frequencies and a tight, percussive attack.

One of the main advantages of a maple neck is its durability. The hardness of the wood makes it resistant to wear and tear, so maple necks are less likely to warp or become damaged over time. Additionally, the stiffness of the wood provides a solid foundation for the guitar's strings, which can help to maintain tuning stability and sustain.

Maple necks are also favored by many players for their fast, smooth playing surface. The smooth finish on a maple neck allows the player's hand to move easily up and down the fretboard, making it ideal for fast and technical playing styles. Some players also find that the brightness of a maple neck can help to cut through a mix, making it a good choice for genres like rock and metal where a strong, articulate tone is important.

Here's an example of the spanky maple tone we're referring to:

Rosewood Neck

Rosewood is a dense, oily wood with a warm, rich tone that is often used for the fingerboards of guitars. Rosewood necks are typically darker in color than maple necks, with a visible grain pattern that can vary from straight and uniform to irregular and complex. Rosewood necks are known for their smooth, mellow tone, which is characterized by a strong low end and a rich, complex midrange.

One of the main advantages of a rosewood neck is its comfort. The porous, oily nature of the wood provides a smooth, tactile surface that feels great under the fingers. This can make it easier to play for extended periods of time, making rosewood necks a good choice for players who value comfort and playability.

Another advantage of a rosewood neck is its tonal complexity. The warm, rich tone of rosewood can add depth and character to a guitar's sound, making it a good choice for genres like blues and jazz where a full, expressive tone is important. Additionally, the porous nature of the wood can help to absorb some of the higher frequencies in a guitar's sound, which can help to reduce harshness and add warmth to the overall tone.

Here's an example of the warm & fat tone we're referring to: 

Conclusion

In the end, the choice between a maple or rosewood neck will largely come down to personal preference and playing style. Maple necks are ideal for players who value durability, bright tone, and fast playing, while rosewood necks are favoured by players who prioritize comfort, tonal complexity, and a warm, rich sound. It's worth noting that many guitars will feature a combination of both woods, with a maple neck and a rosewood fingerboard, for example. This can offer the best of both worlds, allowing players to enjoy the benefits of both woods in a single instrument. Ultimately, the best way to determine which type of neck is right for you is to try out a few different guitars and see which one feels and sounds the best to you.
